name: Whistler Mountain
label: Whistler Mountain
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/2057448487: the OpenStreetMap point 'Whistler Mountain'.
notes: Summit views and the Peak Express area above the village.

text.description: Whistler Mountain rises above the town of Whistler. It sits on the northwestern edge of Garibaldi Provincial Park in the Fitzsimmons Range of the Coast Mountains. It is the location of the Whistler-Blackcomb ski resort, and it was used for the 2010 Winter Olympics. Its Lillooet name is Nsqwítsu. It was once called London Mountain, after a mining claim and the fog that gathers at its base. The name changed to Whistler in the 1960s, after the whistling calls of the marmots that live in the high meadows. The summit is served by the Whistler Peak chair, which makes it one of the most visited summits in British Columbia. The rock is mostly andesite and dacite lava flows with shale, formed around 100 million years ago. That gives the upper slopes a rugged, layered look that shows well on a phone when the light is low and the shadows are long. This spot works best as a wide scene: the mountain filling the top of the frame, with trees or rooftops below to show its size. Use a landmark in front, such as a path or a tree line, to add depth. Zoom in later for ridges and lift lines. Weather changes quickly, so check the sky before you set out.
text.geographic_location: Whistler Mountain rises directly above the town of Whistler in British Columbia and holds the town's ski resort. It lies on the northwestern edge of Garibaldi Provincial Park.
text.directions_text: No Underground, train or tram stop is listed for this spot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole slope and some foreground, then use the default lens (1x) for a more natural look. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for ridges, lift lines and rock detail.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Rainbow Park (northwest shoreline of Alta Lake, on the wooden dock). Lake-level view across Alta Lake to the mountain backdrop, with Whistler and Blackcomb both in frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the skyline on the upper third line, leaving the lower two thirds for trees, paths or buildings that show how big the mountain is. Keep the phone level so the slopes don't tilt. For a second shot, zoom in on one ridge or a lift line.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the sky or the brightest slope to focus, then pull the exposure slider down a little so snow or pale cloud keeps its detail. A panorama can work for the full width of the mountain; sweep slowly and keep the phone level.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a clear day, and go early or in the late afternoon when the light is softer and the slopes show more shape. Midday sun makes the mountain look flat.

text.access_note: The town viewpoints are normally open public space, but the lifts and upper mountain are run by the resort, so check the official site before you go.

name: Peak 2 Peak Gondola
label: Peak 2 Peak Gondola
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'PEAK 2 PEAK Gondola' (2 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position set at the correction gate (pin check 2026-11-18: moved onto the OSM object with the sight's Wikidata ID).
notes: Record-breaking gondola linking Whistler and Blackcomb mountains.

text.description: The Peak 2 Peak Gondola links Whistler Mountain's Roundhouse Lodge with Blackcomb Mountain's Rendezvous Lodge. It was the first lift to join the two mountains. It was built in 2007 and 2008 and carries 28 cabins on a tri-cable system. When it opened it held the world record for the longest free span between towers, at 3.03 kilometres. That record was passed in 2017, but it is still the highest gondola above the ground, at 436 metres. For a photographer, that means a long line of small cabins crossing open air above the valley, with the two mountainsides behind. A good place to photograph it is the Whistler Mountain terminal, outside the station entrance, where you can catch cabins leaving the station with the valley below. The station buildings are covered in a blue, translucent material, which adds a bit of colour to the shot. The short walk across from the Roundhouse can be snowy, so allow a little extra time. Take a few frames as cabins come and go, and include some of the surroundings so the height is clear. If you want a second angle, the Cloudraker Skybridge and Raven's Eye give big mountain views, though the gondola itself may not be in frame from either. Low cloud can hide the views, so check conditions before you set out.
text.geographic_location: Inside the Whistler Blackcomb resort, the gondola spans the valley above Fitzsimmons Creek between Whistler Mountain and Blackcomb Mountain.
text.directions_text: Head for Whistler Village first if you are not already there. The mountains are reached via the Whistler Village or Blackcomb gondolas. Check the official Whistler Blackcomb site for current lift and gondola operating dates before you go. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to show the gondola line with the valley and mountainside around it. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the slope and sky. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out a single cabin on the span.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. It is not at the Whistler Mountain terminal, which is a separate spot outside the station entrance, where cabins can be seen leaving the station.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the line of the cabins along one of them, with the valley filling the background. Wait for a cabin to be clear of other objects so it stands out. For a different view, the Cloudraker Skybridge and Raven's Eye offer mountain panoramas, but the gondola may not be in frame from either.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on a cabin to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if bright sky or snow is washing out the picture. A Live Photo can catch the cabins moving, and panorama mode suits the wide valley view.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a clear daylight window, as low cloud can hide the valley and the far side. Check the weather and summit conditions on the day.

text.access_note: The gondola is a ticketed lift, and summer access depends on the ticket and season, so check the official site before you go.

name: Whistler Village
label: Whistler Village
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Whistler Olympic Plaza' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Whistler Olympic Plaza' (node/3269531962): point; moved 5 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OSM W50677442 (Whistler Village Gondola): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Pedestrian heart of the resort with shops, restaurants and the gondola bases.

text.description: Whistler Village is the setting for this shot, and the classic way to photograph it is from Whistler Olympic Plaza. Here the Olympic Rings sit in the foreground, with the village roofs and snowy mountains rising behind them. It is the village postcard shot: a clear mountain backdrop, with plaza greenery and water features to give the picture a foreground. One guide notes there is enough room to back up and fit the rings, the trees and the mountain into a single frame, so take a few steps back before you shoot. The plaza can be busy during events and may have stage setups, so look around before choosing your spot. If you have time for a second picture, wander into the village lanes. Timber-framed storefronts, cobbled paths and street life look good with the mountains showing above the rooftops. The Covered Bridge is a quieter option: a rustic wooden bridge with the icy blue creek below and mountains beyond. The village gondola, the subject of this entry, lies south of the plaza. The plaza is the better place to stand for a view that takes in the whole scene. Keep your phone steady, tap the screen on the rings to set focus, and check the edges of the frame for passers-by before you press the shutter.
text.geographic_location: The viewpoint is Whistler Olympic Plaza, in Whistler Village, about 676 m north of the village gondola. The village sits below the snowy mountains that appear behind the Olympic Rings.
text.directions_text: Reach Whistler Olympic Plaza on foot from the village. The village gondola is about 676 m to the south of the plaza. Once you are in the plaza, look for the Olympic Rings and walk a few steps back from them to fit in the mountains. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to get the rings, the village and the mountains in one frame. If the plaza is crowded and you cannot step back, switch to ultra-wide (0.5x). To pick out the mountains behind the village, try telephoto (2x or 3x, depending on your phone).
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Whistler Olympic Plaza (in front of the Olympic Rings, stepping back for the wider frame). The Olympic Rings in the foreground with the village and snowy mountains rising behind them.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the rings on one of the lower lines, with the mountains filling the upper part. Use the plaza greenery or the water features as a foreground. For a different view, the village lanes and the Covered Bridge make good alternatives: the lanes show timber-framed storefronts with mountains above the rooftops, and the bridge shows the blue creek below with mountains beyond.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the rings to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky and snow keep their detail. In the evening, use night mode only if the lights look dim, and hold the phone steady against your body or a rail.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Evening, when the village lights and the mountain silhouettes work together.

text.access_note: The plaza is an open public square, but events may add stage setups, so look around on arrival.

name: Audain Art Museum
label: Audain Art Museum
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/499207972: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Audain Art Museum' (151 m across).
notes: Modern museum of British Columbia art, set among the trees.

text.description:
The Audain Art Museum is a private museum in Whistler that holds the collection of Michael Audain, with a large permanent display of art from coastal British Columbia. It was designed by Patkau Architects and opened in 2016. It is a long building, and it was shaped to sit quietly among the mature spruce and cedar on its forested site. Only a single tree was removed in the first phase of construction. The cladding is an intentionally recessive colour that recedes into the shadows of the trees, so the building seems to fade into them. That makes it a calm, moody subject rather than a bright postcard one. The site is on the Fitzsimmons Creek floodplain, and the design was shaped by the site's flood risk and Whistler's heavy snowfall. The building has also won a string of architecture awards, including a 2018 RIBA Award for International Excellence.

For a phone photo, the appeal is the contrast between the simple, recessive walls and the tall trees around them. Look for long horizontal lines, wood textures and the way the forest closes in. The building is big, so you will not fit all of it in one frame without stepping well back. Go for a few separate pictures instead: one wide view, one of a detail, and one with a tree trunk framing the edge. Check the official site before you go for rules on photography inside, as many galleries limit it.
text.geographic_location: In Whistler, British Columbia, on a wooded site in the Fitzsimmons Creek floodplain. The building is set among spruce and cedar trees.
text.directions_text: No public transport stop is listed for this spot; head for the Audain Art Museum itself. The phone icon on the map marks the centre of the building outline, so walk out to the edge of the building or the grounds and step well back to frame it. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the long building and the surrounding trees. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural view of the walls and entrance. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for cladding textures and details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Walk out to the edge of the building or the grounds and step well back to frame the whole length.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the roof and wall edges with them so the building looks level. Use a tree trunk or branches at one side as a frame. Take a wide shot first, then move in for close-ups of wood, edges and reflections.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: The walls blend into the shadows of the trees, so tap on a mid-tone area to focus, then slide the exposure slider down a touch if the sky turns white. If the phone offers it, a single extra shot with a lighter exposure helps keep detail in the shadows.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft, even light on a cloudy day or in the morning suits the recessive cladding and avoids harsh patches under the trees.

text.access_note: This is a private museum, so entry is likely ticketed and may have set opening times; check the official site before you go.

name: Lost Lake
label: Lost Lake
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Lost Lake Park' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Lost Lake Park' (relation/2312609): middle (211 m across).

notes: Forest lake just north of the village, popular for walks and swimming.

text.description: Lost Lake is a lake in Whistler, British Columbia, set in woodland inside Lost Lake Park. The park is part of the municipal park system and doubles as cross-country skiing trails in winter. It photographs well because the sheltered water is often calm, so the forest and the Whistler and Blackcomb mountains can show up as reflections. The best-known frame is from the floating dock, with the lake in front of you, trees down both sides and the peaks beyond. The lake has several public docks, and the park's swimming docks were historically the nude sunbathing area, so be mindful of who is in your frame. For a quieter picture, walk along the shoreline, where the forest and lake fill the frame with fewer people in it. The sandy beach is also worth a look, with mountain reflections that guides recommend at golden hour. Evening light is the favourite time, and the summer months are busy, so arrive early or late if you want a clear view of the water. Parking nearby is limited, and parking and shuttle arrangements can vary, so check on the day.
text.geographic_location: Lost Lake sits in Lost Lake Park, part of Whistler's municipal park system in British Columbia. The view from the dock looks across the water towards Whistler and Blackcomb mountains.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for the park, and parking nearby is limited. From the parking lot, follow the path up the right-hand side of the lake to the floating dock. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the lake, the reflections and the mountains together. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the dock planks in the foreground, or to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the peaks across the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Lost Lake Park (the floating dock, reached by going up the right-hand side of the lake from the parking lot). Reflective lake view across the water toward Whistler and Blackcomb mountains, framed by forest.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the water's edge on a lower line, so that the sky and the reflection each take up about half of the picture. Hold the phone low and level, and keep the trees on both sides as a natural frame. If the dock is crowded, a quieter alternative is the shoreline, which gives forest and lake views with fewer people in the shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the mountains to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky keeps its colour and the reflections stay clear. Wait for a still moment before pressing the shutter, since ripples spoil the mirror effect. A Live Photo can help you pick the calmest frame afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Guides recommend the evening for good light on the calm water, and golden hour for the sandy beach. Early or late in the day is also likely to be quieter in the busy summer months.

text.access_note: Lost Lake Park is a public park, but parking is limited and details may change, so check the official site before you go.

name: Whistler Olympic Plaza
label: Olympic Plaza
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Whistler Olympic Plaza' (4 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OSM N3269531962 (Whistler Olympic Plaza): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Plaza with the Olympic rings, used for the 2010 Winter Games medal ceremonies.

text.description:
Whistler Olympic Plaza is an open public square in Whistler, and its best-known photo is the five Olympic Rings at the entrance, with the plaza and the mountain backdrop rising behind them. That layering of bold foreground, open space and mountains is why it works so well on a phone. The rings are the obvious subject, and the mountains give the picture a clear sense of place.

Guides suggest using the rock podium in front of the rings as a camera stand for group shots. Exactly where the rings sit is worth checking on the day. The City of Whistler places them at the entrance to the former medals plaza, while other guides say they are beside the plaza. Either way, you will find them near the entrance.

If you want a second picture without the rings, turn towards the plaza's open lawn and stage, with trees and mountains rising behind. This is a quieter, wider view.

In winter, skating rinks and the playground can block the lawn and ground-level angles. In summer, concerts and events can crowd the plaza. Check current event schedules before you go, and allow a little patience if a group is posing at the rings. Stand a few steps back so the rings and the mountains both fit in one frame.
text.geographic_location: Whistler Olympic Plaza is in Whistler, a public plaza with a lawn and stage, and the Olympic Rings stand at its entrance.
text.directions_text: Head for Whistler Olympic Plaza and look for the Olympic Rings at the plaza entrance. No station or tram stop is listed for this spot. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) so the rings and the mountain backdrop sit together. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) for big group shots when you cannot step back. Use 2x on the telephoto for a tighter view of the mountains behind the plaza, without the rings in the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here the five rings fill the foreground and the plaza and mountains rise behind them. Guides suggest using the rock podium in front of the rings as a camera stand for group shots.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the rings on one of the lower lines, leaving the mountains in the upper part of the frame. Hold the phone level so the rings do not lean. If you want a different view, face the open lawn and stage, with trees and mountains behind, and leave the rings out.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the rings to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is washing out. For group shots, try a Live Photo so you can pick the best moment from the motion.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Winter is the best season, when the plaza can glow in alpenglow. Check the event schedule first, as summer concerts and events can crowd the plaza and winter rinks can block some angles.

text.access_note: The rings viewpoint is free to visit, but events can affect access to parts of the plaza, so check the official site before you go.

name: Alta Lake
label: Alta Lake
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Rainbow Park' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Rainbow Park' (way/24671612): middle (551 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/2382440: large area 'Alta Lake' (2362 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Large lake west of the village with mountain reflections at sunset.

text.description: Alta Lake is the long, quiet lake on Whistler's west side, and the best-known view of it is from Rainbow Park on its northwest shore. The pier works as a leading line: it draws the eye out over the lake and up to the peaks, which makes a simple, balanced phone photo. The lake was first called Summit Lake and was renamed to avoid confusion with the many other Summit Lakes in British Columbia. Its new name comes from a Spanish word meaning "high up". It sits at about 642 metres above sea level, stretches roughly 2.2 km from north to south, and covers about 1.1 square kilometres. At the north end you can still find cabins from the old Rainbow Lodge resort. For the calmest water and the warmest light, go early in the morning or around sunset. Mist on the lake can add atmosphere, and in autumn the morning sun can cut through it. Rainbow Park is one of Whistler's busiest parks in summer, so expect people on the pier and be ready to wait a moment for a clear frame. If you want a second view, Lakeside Park looks across open water toward the surrounding peaks, with rushes and shoreline in the foreground.
text.geographic_location: Alta Lake lies on the west side of Whistler, in the area now known as Westside. The photo spot is Rainbow Park, on the lake's northwest shore.
text.directions_text: Start from Whistler's Westside, the original Alta Lake community, and head for Rainbow Park on Alta Lake Road (5778 Alta Lake Rd). From there the lake is about 670 m to the south, roughly an 8 to 9 minute walk. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) so the pier, water and mountains all fit naturally. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the pier to look longer and fill the foreground. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pull Whistler and Blackcomb closer and make a tighter mountain shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Rainbow Park (northwest shoreline of Alta Lake; use the long pier that runs out over the water). Whistler and Blackcomb mountains rising behind the lake, with the pier as a leading line into the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the pier along a line so it leads into the lake, with the mountains in the upper part of the frame. Crouch slightly to bring the planks and water closer to the lens. For a different view, Lakeside Park gives open water and shoreline rushes in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the mountains to focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so the sky keeps its colour and the water stays rich. On a still morning, hold your phone steady and take a few frames to get one without ripples or people.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or sunset, when the light is warm and the lake can be mirror-calm. Morning mist can be lovely in autumn.

text.access_note: Rainbow Park is a public park and no charge is known for it, but check the official site before you go for current conditions.
